title: You weren't chosen by God. Now what?
summary: A long self-improvement and philosophy essay built on the sports manga Eyeshield 21, using its characters (Sena, Sakuraba, Unsui, Hiruma, Habashira, Kakei, Taki, Apollo, Mizumachi, Yukimitsu) as archetypes for how an average, ungifted person should respond to not being chosen by fate. NH mixes in his own story of going from a weak, bullied 110 lb teen to a lifter, his swimming ego-death and his bike-climb turning point, and argues that mediocrity is self-inflicted, effort guarantees nothing, and the only answer is to keep climbing.
claims: Social media algorithms only show genetic freaks, which shifts what feels normal and makes perfectly average lifters believe they have bad genetics
Believing you have trash genetics becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy: you give up preemptively, get poor results, and take them as proof you were right
As a kid he was told his genetics meant there was no point trying to build muscle; he believed it, and without an outside spark he would still be a 130 lb adult with spaghetti arms
At 14 he was 5'5 and 110 lb, lost arm wrestling to small girls, could not do a single push-up or hold a leg raise
Neck training has made his favourite shirts too tight around the collar
He was mostly raised by conflict-avoiding women who kept him in a protective cocoon; protection from adversity prevented him from growing
Pain is unpleasant, but the consequences of never facing pain are far worse than the pain itself; realizing this is when a boy becomes a man
Wanting to grow, expand and accumulate power is embracing life; shrinking from pain and adversity is renouncing life and leads toward depression
His turning point: one summer on a bike he kept failing a climb, realized that if he got off that day he would get off every day, refused to stop and finished it
Change is fractional and slow; old habits and self-limiting beliefs return if you stop watching them, so self-improvement is trading bad habits and beliefs for good ones
Mediocrity is a self-inflicted state you choose because it is comfortable
Self-improvement is a climb where you cannot stay still: you go up or you go down, and the direction you choose matters more than winning or losing
Calling yourself a realist to justify not trying is usually cowardice disguised as enlightenment, and the proof is that such people are miserable
A good decision leaves a peaceful feeling; a choice that keeps gnawing at you is probably eroding you
Ambition without action leads to despair: if you cannot be Caesar you end up unable to accept being yourself (Kierkegaard)
Potential is volatile and genetics evolve with your choices; someone who works much harder can end up looking gifted when he is not
Lifters who say ten years of training was all for nothing are rejecting real progress because it does not match a grandiose image; you are owed nothing for trying
Your expectations exist only in your head; if reality falls short the only fix is to blame yourself and work twice as hard
Intermediates who say they stopped progressing are just progressing slower, like a car dropping from 100 to 20 mph; most of the climb is slow
Self-pitying blackpilled people he meets are almost always average; truly disadvantaged people tend to have champion mindsets because they have no choice

A lifter at his old university gym had a nerve condition that blocked upper-body growth: 500 lb squat but 30 lb curl and 160-170 lb bench; he trained twice a day at two gyms, never complained and was loved by everyone
There is no karma: lazy people with gifts will outperform you; resenting it breeds jealousy, which fills the fitness industry and only hurts you
Complaining about your genetics has never improved anyone's life, and there will always be someone better than you
Trendy renunciation philosophies can become a mask for passivity; ignoring your desires does not remove them, they fester and grow
If you struggle for years to deadlift three plates you will never be very strong; accept those cards and find another front, as Hiruma does with strategy after benching only 70 kg after years
Growing up weak he became a fox rather than a lion, winning through rules and strategy instead of direct confrontation, and still prefers that path
He refuses to coach because too many clients gave up after two months of his help
If you are self-driven, find a community of people striving for excellence; he has seen people doing everything right turn into losers to fit in with losers
A whole year of training for only 0.1 s on the 40-yard dash is still improvement worth pursuing; trade a 4 of spades for a 5 whenever you can
Effort does not guarantee success; luck and environment matter, and you may get only pain for believing in yourself, yet it is still worth it
Fear of being laughed at in the gym is a fragile ego; everyone at a high level looked foolish once, so pay that price early instead of staying mediocre
He was the best swimmer at national level from 8 to 12, stopped training for 3 years thinking he was gifted, and at 15 came last behind the kids he used to lap
He has no real natural talent for lifting yet is better at it than he ever was at swimming, because of hard work
It is better to smash your own ego than to have someone else do it, because you can rebuild from a healthier base
Learning how to lose is a more valuable skill than winning, because you will lose far more than you win and the cycle never ends
Excellent people are often rejected by the mediocre majority, which glorifies the traits that comfort its mediocrity (Nietzsche's slave morality)
He was pushed to be a bookworm because people decided he was cerebral, and realized almost too late that he wanted to be physical
Ability is the sum of experience: a 24-year-old after two years of lifting cannot compare himself to someone who has wrestled 3 hours a day since age 6 and call him gifted
No one is made for something; you choose a pursuit, stick to it, and that makes you made for it
It is never too late to start lifting at 23: in three years you will have three years of training behind you
Eyeshield 21 includes a science-based versus Spartan training arc relevant to lifters; read the manga, the anime is a poor, filler-heavy partial adaptation
